newsitem.title: GERMANY: ECOFIN would give ECB scope to talk -- Lamfalussy.
newsitem.headline: ECOFIN would give ECB scope to talk -- Lamfalussy.

text.p: European Monetary Institute (EMI) President Alexandre Lamfalussy said he believed the future European Central Bank (ECB) could have useful dialogue with a group of ECOFIN ministers representing only the Euro area.

Speaking to journalists on Monday evening, and stressing that his views were personal and did not represent those of the EMI council, Lamfalussy said such an arrangement could benefit the ECB and would not endanger its independence.
"There is a need for an organised dialogue between the governments and the European Central Bank. The current ECOFIN may not be sufficient," Lamfalussy said.

Lamfalussy added that the Maastricht Treaty made no provision whatsoever for what he called "a sort of inner ECOFIN", being based on the presumption that a large majority of EU states would take part in monetary union from its launch.
But, he said, there was now a clear incentive for ministers representing countries inside the Euro area to meet and discuss strategy after the single currency launch in January 1999.
"We will have one monetary policy for six, seven, eight or ten members and a fiscal policy for 15. This is a simple arithmetical problem," Lamfalussy said.

Lamfalussy said his ideas were by no means designed to give outright support to French proposals for an informal G-7 style meeting of European Union finance ministers to discuss issues related to monetary policy under monetary union.
"I have said very explicitly that I do not wish to enter the current debate," he said.

French proposals for a so-called "stability council" to coordinate economic policies inside European monetary union have been attacked by the Bundesbank as an assault on the European Central Bank's independence.
Lamfalussy said his ideas did not carry such a risk.

"We cannot play with central bank independence. If the objective (of a council) is as a means of influencing the central bank, then I would say no. But if this is a way of organising a dialogue, then it would be useful," he said.

The ECB would be in any case far more capable than any existing central banks to maintain its independence, since its mandate to focus on price stability was, uniquely, written into an international contract.
Moreover, progress toward central bank independence throughout Europe was, Lamfalussy said, far more advanced today than it was in the early 1990s.

"When you have an organisation whose mandate is extraordinarily well-defined, people who are appointed by...all the countries involved, with eight-year mandates to preserve price stability, I think there is a very strong ability to resist (political pressures)," he said.
The EMI President conceded, however, that ministers of countries likely to be outside the Euro area would not initially welcome the idea.
Nonetheless, he said, "it is also in the interest of the European Central Bank to be able to talk to someone."

In a hypothetical example of a case where such dialogue could come into play, Lamfalussy cited the case of a large Euro area state with a two percent budget surplus that decided to switch to a two percent deficit, a move which would satisfy Maastricht Treaty criteria but pressure the ECB.
"The question for the ECB will be: will we let this happen or try to persuade governments (of other EMU states) to intervene?," Lamfalussy asked.
